title: It Didn't Know It Was Dead

post.author: u/third_shift_tom
post.title: Fencing is on now. Our database refused every write from a machine we retired in March. Three of our drivers still got its texts.

blocks.text: Tom again, night operator at Kestrelmoor Freight. Three machines, app-1 to app-3, give each order to a truck and text its driver. A program called the Head of Shift, in the trade a coordinator, hands them the work.

Work comes in batches of orders, each lent with a lease: ownership with an expiry, like a library loan. The Head of Shift grants a batch to one machine for 60 seconds, timed on its own clock. The machine renews in time, or the lease expires and the batch goes to another machine.
Every grant carries a number called a token, from the one counter from Part 1 that only ever goes up. A renewal keeps its token.

The orders database stores the token with every write. Fencing is on now: it refuses a write whose token is lower than the newest it holds for that batch. It's a gate: it lets only the newest owner through.

Tonight app-2 froze again at 2:13: it stopped answering. Thirty seconds, declared dead, orders handed to app-3 with token 34. When app-2 woke up it tried to finish order #4471 with token 33. The database said no. I was so relieved I almost missed the next line in the log. At 2:51 a write arrived with token 9, for batch #1102. We haven't issued token 9 since March. It came from a machine called app-0. We don't have an app-0.
Each line: time, log, machine, request for batch #1102, token, answer.

02:51:02  database       app-0  write #2630  token 9  REFUSED, newest 10
02:51:12  database       app-0  write #2631  token 9  REFUSED, newest 10
02:51:22  database       app-0  write #2632  token 9  REFUSED, newest 10
02:51:40  Head of Shift  app-0  renew lease  token 9  REFUSED, closed 15 Mar

At 03:06 Mahalia, a driver, texted me a photo: a boarded-up house on Hatherley Road. "Got a job here at 02:51. Same house as March. Nobody has lived here for years." Chidinma and Bjarke got March orders at 02:51 too. Texts never touch the database: a machine hands a texting service the message. It checks no token.

app-0 was retired in March. Tonight Dumisani, our backup contractor, ran a restore test. Our backups are snapshots: a saved copy of a whole machine, disk and memory, at one moment. A restore: pick a snapshot, pick a network, start it. The copy carries on from that moment.
He picked app-0's March snapshot. It still carried March's network label: live, not test. At 02:51:00 app-0 woke beside our real machines.
Machines set their clocks by asking a time server: time sync. We paused it on purpose for the March move, when the snapshot was taken. So app-0's clock woke reading 02:08:20, Sunday 15 March.

March's Head of Shift log: at 02:08:00 app-0 got lease 9 on batch #1102. At 02:08:20 we took the snapshot and shut it down. At 02:09:00 lease 9 expired; app-1 got the batch with token 10, texted those three drivers, closed it. Mahalia found that house empty then. The address was fixed next day.
By app-0's own clock, lease 9 still had 40 seconds. It used them: three writes, three texts. Then its renewal was refused.

Row two, the Head of Shift: batch 1102 has been closed since March. Row three, texts reaching drivers: at 02:51:02, 02:51:12 and 02:51:22. Red on the first row is lease 9 as app-0's own clock saw it: valid until 02:51:40, because its clock said 02:08:20 on Sunday 15 March. On the Head of Shift's clock, batch #1102 closed on 15 March. Each mark is one order: a write refused with token 9, and a text that reached a driver anyway: #2630 to Chidinma, #2631 to Mahalia, #2632 to Bjarke.

blocks.text: Dumisani switched app-0 off at 03:14. Next restore test: Tuesday 3 November. What should we change before then?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Any stop in a running machine, for whatever reason, is called a pause. A machine that carries on with work it no longer owns, because it doesn't know it was replaced, is called a zombie. Before you choose, read your logs again. Which of app-0's actions passed the database, and which never went near it? How long was app-0's pause, measured on the Head of Shift's clock? When app-0 decided its lease was still good, whose clock did it read? And at 02:51, who knew app-0 was running?

replies.author: u/third_shift_tom
replies.text: Passed the database: the three writes, all refused. Never went near it: the three texts. The pause, on the Head of Shift's clock, was 226 days, from 02:08:20 on 15 March to 02:51:00 tonight. app-0 read its own clock. And nobody knew it was running. Dumisani thought it was on the test network.

comments.author: u/asks_first_annukka
comments.text: The database refused the writes, so fencing worked. The bug is that app-0 trusted its own clock. Make every machine ask the Head of Shift "is my lease still valid?" right before it acts. A machine that checks its lease before acting can't go wrong, and you need no new parts.

replies.author: u/third_shift_tom
replies.text: Dumisani likes this one. One question per order, and nothing new to run.

comments.author: u/old_racks_rhiannedd
comments.text: I ran machine rooms for twenty years. We fenced the machine, not the data: before a frozen machine's work went to another, we cut its power at a power switch it couldn't touch, so it could never wake and act. Old practice. It still works.

reply.prompt: The next restore test is on Tuesday 3 November. What should Kestrelmoor change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Send every text through a gate that refuses tokens older than the newest it has seen.
options.part2: On Friday 30 October we put a gate in front of the texting service: a small program every text must pass. It keeps the newest token for each batch, starting from the database's record, and refuses a text with an older one. The Head of Shift now tells each machine when its lease ends on the Head of Shift's own clock, and each text carries a ticket number, its order number plus "dispatch", so a repeat is dropped: Rule 3. In the sim, replaying 27 October with the gate: app-0's three writes refused by the database, its three texts refused at the gate, 9 below 10. Texts that reached drivers: 0. On Tuesday 3 November Dumisani ran the restore test on the test network, with the label checked by hand. Mahalia's phone stayed quiet.
options.senior: Fencing protects only the places that check the token. Put the same check at every place that acts on the world: the database, the texting service, anything that sends a truck. A gate there keeps the newest token per batch and refuses older ones, whoever sends them and whatever code they run, which is why it stops a machine restored from March. Time every lease on the coordinator's clock, never the holder's, and give each action a ticket number so a repeat is dropped. Then a paused or restored machine can act all it likes and nothing reaches a driver.

options.text: Power off any frozen machine before its work goes to another, so no old owner can act.
options.verdict: Trade-off: only the machines you know
options.part2: On Friday 30 October we wired every machine to a power switch the Head of Shift controls: before it hands a batch on, it switches the old owner off. In the sim, replaying 27 October with the rule on: app-0 wasn't frozen, nobody knew it was running, and its batch had been handed on in March. Three writes refused, three texts reached drivers. Then I read March's log again. The rule had already happened to app-0 once: on 15 March we shut it down before batch #1102 went to app-1. The restore switched it back on.
options.senior: Fence the machine, not the data, is real practice: cutting a machine's power before its work moves on stops a known paused machine for certain, and cluster tools such as Pacemaker do exactly that. But it reaches only machines the coordinator knows about and can switch off, it needs a power switch the machine can't block, and it does nothing about a copy started later from a snapshot. Keep it as a layer, and still check the token at every place that acts.

options.text: Have each machine ask the coordinator if its lease is still valid right before it acts.
options.part2: On Friday 30 October we changed the code on app-1, app-2 and app-3: before each write or text, ask the Head of Shift whether the lease is still valid. In the sim, replaying 27 October: app-0 runs the code saved in its March snapshot, which never asks. Three texts reached drivers. Then I gave app-0's copy the new code too, the kindest case. With no pause it sent nothing. But if the snapshot falls between a "yes" and the text that yes allowed, the copy wakes and sends it: one text still reached a driver.
options.senior: Asking before acting narrows the window but can't close it. A machine can pause at any point, including between the answer and the action, for a memory clean-up, a frozen host or a snapshot, and then act on a yes that is no longer true. This is Kleppmann's central example. And a check that lives inside a machine's code never reaches a machine running older code. The check has to happen where the action lands: the receiving side compares the token.

options.text: Lengthen every lease from 60 seconds to 10 minutes, so no owner's lease runs out early.
options.part2: On Friday 30 October every lease went from 60 seconds to 10 minutes. None of that reaches app-0's March copy: its lease 9 was granted for 60 seconds. In the sim, replaying 27 October as if 10-minute leases had been in place in March: the snapshot was taken 20 seconds into lease 9, so app-0's own clock says it has 580 seconds left, not 40. It still sends three texts, and it believes it owns batch #1102 until 03:00:40. And a machine that really dies now keeps its batch for up to 10 minutes before anyone else may touch it.
options.senior: A longer lease changes how long a holder believes it owns something, not whether that belief is true. app-0's clock was 226 days wrong, so no lease length helps, and any pause longer than the lease still makes a zombie. Longer leases also leave a dead machine's work waiting longer. Choose the lease length for how fast you want to recover, and get safety from tokens checked at every place that acts.

sim.title: Replay app-0's minute on the live network
sim.lede: You're Tom on Tuesday 27 October 2026 at 02:50:00, before app-0 wakes. As given data: on Sunday 15 March the Head of Shift granted app-0 lease 9 on batch #1102 at 02:08:00 for 60 seconds; the snapshot was taken at 02:08:20; at 02:09:00 app-1 got the batch with token 10, texted the three drivers and closed it. The database's newest token for #1102 is 10. Tonight at 02:51:00 app-0 wakes from the snapshot with three orders left, one every 10 seconds from 02:51:02: #2630 (Chidinma), #2631 (Mahalia, Hatherley Road) and #2632 (Bjarke). For each, it writes to the database and texts the driver. The texting service keeps ticket numbers for 30 days. The settings for app-0's clock, how it judges its lease, the pause after an answer and the lease length apply to app-0's copy as if they had been in place before March; tonight's real copy reads its own clock and held a 60-second lease. Set them, then play 02:50 to 02:52.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play it as built: 3 writes refused by the database, 3 texts reached drivers. Turn on the gate at texting: 0. Power off before handover with app-0 unknown: still 3; with app-0 known: 0. Ask the Head of Shift before each act: 0 with no pause, 1 when the snapshot falls between a yes and its act. 10-minute leases: still 3, and app-0 believes it owns the batch for 580 seconds. Ticket numbers alone: still 3, because March's were forgotten after 30 days. A synced clock: 0.

explain.oneLine: Fencing worked where it was checked. app-0, a March snapshot started on the live network, read its own stopped clock, believed lease 9 had 40 seconds left and acted: the database refused token 9, but the texting service checked nothing. Check the token at every place that acts, and time leases on the coordinator's clock.

steps.title: A lease, step by step.
steps.text: A lease is ownership with an expiry, granted and timed by the coordinator. First, the coordinator grants a batch to one machine for 60 seconds and notes the end on its own clock. Second, the machine renews before the end; each new grant gets the next token from the one counter, and a renewal keeps its token. Third, if renewals stop, the lease expires on the coordinator's clock. Fourth, the coordinator hands the batch on with the next token. What goes wrong: the holder judges the end on its own clock, which can be paused, wrong or, like app-0's, 226 days behind. The holder's idea of its lease is only a guess; the coordinator's record is the truth.

steps.title: Tokens and fencing: the receiver decides.
steps.text: A fencing token is a number that grows with every grant. In steps: the coordinator issues it with the lease; the holder sends it with every action; the receiver remembers the newest token it has seen for that batch and refuses anything lower. Kestrelmoor's database did this and refused token 9 three times, because it held 10. It works whatever the sender believes, which is the point: the decision moves from the possibly confused sender to the receiver. What goes wrong: a receiver that doesn't check. Kleppmann notes that fencing needs the storage server to take an active role in checking tokens.

steps.title: Zombies after pauses.
steps.text: A zombie is a machine still acting on work it no longer owns, because it can't see that it was replaced. A pause makes one: a memory clean-up, a frozen host, or a snapshot started months later. Here the pause was 226 days long, and app-0 woke mid-step with lease 9 and a clock reading 02:08:20 on 15 March. Asking first doesn't save it: check-then-act fails when a pause falls between the check and the act, and a snapshot can fall exactly there. And a machine restored from an old copy runs the old code, so any fix made since never reaches it.

steps.title: Every place that acts checks the token.
steps.text: The texting service is a second door out to the world, and it had no check. The fix puts a gate in front of it. First, the gate copies the newest token per batch from the database's record. Second, every text carries its batch and token. Third, the gate refuses any token older than the newest it holds. Fourth, each text carries a ticket number, its order plus dispatch, so a repeated text is dropped (Rule 3). What goes wrong: a third door added later, such as email, that skips the gate. Restore tests also get their own step: check the network label by hand, and run on the test network.

steps.title: Fence the machine: the older practice.
steps.text: Before tokens were common, clusters fenced the machine itself: before handing a frozen machine's work on, cut its power through a power switch it can't reach, so it can never act again. Pacemaker still does this; it is often called STONITH. It is certain for a machine you know and can reach. It does nothing for a machine nobody knew was running, like app-0, and it needs that switch to work when everything else is failing. Use it as a layer, never instead of tokens.

diagram.aria: The fix replayed for 27 October. In March the Head of Shift grants app-0 lease 9 until 02:09:00. app-0 is paused by the snapshot for 226 days. At 02:09:00 in March the Head of Shift hands batch 1102 to app-1 with token 10. Tonight app-0 sends a write for order 2630 with token 9 to the database, which refuses it because the newest is 10. app-0 sends the text for order 2630 with token 9 to the texting gate, which refuses it too. Outcome: 0 texts reach drivers.

explain.caption: The fix, replayed for 27 October. The snapshot is a pause of 226 days between lease 9 and app-0's next step, and meanwhile the batch moved on to token 10. When app-0 wakes, both places that act check the token: the database refuses the write and the gate refuses the text. Orders #2631 and #2632 go the same way.

fix.title: The fix: check the token at every place that acts, and time leases on the coordinator's clock
fix.text: Put a gate in front of the texting service, and in front of any other way the machines act on the world. It keeps the newest token per batch, filled from the database's record, and refuses any text with an older token. Have the Head of Shift tell each holder when its lease ends by the Head of Shift's own clock, so no machine judges its lease on its own clock. Give every text a ticket number, the order number plus dispatch, so a repeat is dropped (Rule 3). Make restore tests run only on the test network, with the label checked by hand before the copy starts, and keep time sync on in every saved copy. Keep the power switch rule for frozen machines you know about, as a second layer.

limits: A gate guards only the doors that have one. A new way to act on the world, such as email to customers, needs the same check, or it is a way out for every zombie.
The gate must know the newest token before an old owner's text arrives. That's why it starts from the database's record; a gate that learns only from texts it sees would have let token 9 through.
Ticket numbers are kept for a while, not for ever. March's were forgotten after 30 days, so a ticket number alone could not tell that tonight's texts were repeats.

explain.seniorTake: No machine can be sure it still owns anything: it can be paused at any moment, its clock can be wrong, and it can be a copy started from months ago. So never let the holder decide. The coordinator grants and times every lease on its own clock and stamps each grant with a growing token, and every place that acts on the world, the database, the texting service, payments, email, refuses a token older than the newest it has seen. Asking first and longer leases only change how often a zombie acts, not whether it can. Powering off a frozen machine is a good extra layer when you know the machine and can reach its switch. And treat a restored backup as a live machine until proven otherwise: restore onto an isolated network, with time sync on.

realWorld.title: Kleppmann, 2016: a lease is a lock with a timeout
realWorld.text: Martin Kleppmann writes: "The lock has a timeout (i.e. it is a lease), which is always a good idea (otherwise a crashed client could end up holding a lock forever and never releasing it)." Then the danger: "However, if the GC pause lasts longer than the lease expiry period, and the client doesn’t realise that it has expired, it may go ahead and make some unsafe change." GC is a memory clean-up; app-0's pause was a snapshot.

realWorld.title: Kleppmann: checking first doesn't help
realWorld.text: "You cannot fix this problem by inserting a check on the lock expiry just before writing back to storage." A pause can come at any point, "including the point that is maximally inconvenient for you (between the last check and the write operation)." That is option 2's flaw.

realWorld.title: Kleppmann: fencing tokens, 33 and 34
realWorld.text: "In this context, a fencing token is simply a number that increases (e.g. incremented by the lock service) every time a client acquires the lock." His example: "Client 1 acquires the lease and gets a token of 33, but then it goes into a long pause and the lease expires." The storage server "rejects the request with token 33." And he adds: "Note this requires the storage server to take an active role in checking tokens".

realWorld.title: Kleppmann: leases lean on timing
realWorld.text: On a lock built from timeouts: "if the timing issues become as large as the time-to-live, the algorithm fails." app-0's timing issue was 226 days against a 60-second lease.

realWorld.title: Pacemaker: fence the machine
realWorld.text: The Pacemaker cluster manual defines it: "Fencing is the ability to make a node unable to run resources, even when that node is unresponsive to cluster commands." It explains the usual way: "since the most common fencing method is cutting power to the node." A node is one machine in the cluster.

asked: What is a fencing token, and where must it be checked?
Why can't a process trust its own lease?
What happens when an old snapshot boots on the live network?
interview.answer: A lease is ownership with an expiry. The coordinator grants it, times it on its own clock, takes renewals, lets it expire and hands the work on. A fencing token is a number the coordinator issues with each grant, always higher than the last. The holder sends it with every action, and the receiver remembers the newest token it has seen and refuses anything lower. It must be checked at every place that acts on the world, not only the database: the texting service, the email sender, the payment call. A process can't trust its own lease because it can't see its own pauses. A memory clean-up, a frozen host or a snapshot can stop it for any length of time, its clock can be wrong, and it may have been replaced while stopped. Even asking the coordinator right before acting fails, because a pause can fall between the answer and the action. An old snapshot booted on the live network is the extreme case: it wakes mid-step, believes it holds the leases it held then, and acts. Fencing stops it where tokens are checked, and nothing stops it where they aren't. I'd tell the story of a freight company whose March snapshot woke on the live network: the database refused token 9 three times, and three drivers still got texts, one to a house empty for years. Then the fix: a gate with the newest token per batch in front of every way out, leases timed by the coordinator, ticket numbers on each action, and restore tests on an isolated network. Powering off a frozen machine is a good extra layer, but only for machines you know about.

A number that comes with each grant and grows by one each time. At Kestrelmoor each batch counts its own: lease 9, then 10.
The program that keeps Kestrelmoor's orders. It stores the token with every write.
A change sent to the database, such as marking an order as sent to a truck.

The outside service that sends Kestrelmoor's texts. A machine hands it a phone number and a message. It checked no token.
Stopped answering for a while, with nothing visibly wrong, then carried on as if no time had passed.
The Head of Shift's verdict after 30 seconds of silence from a machine: its batch goes to another machine at once, without waiting for the lease to run out. Silence or expiry, whichever comes first.
Any stop in a running machine: a memory clean-up, a frozen host, or a snapshot started later. The machine can't see its own pauses.
A machine still acting on work it no longer owns, because it doesn't know it was replaced. app-0 was one.
A saved copy kept so things can be put back after a loss.
A saved copy of a whole machine, its disk and memory, at one moment. Started again, it carries on from that moment.

The name saying which network a restored machine joins: live or test. app-0's snapshot kept its March label, live.

A network cut off from the live one, for restore tests and trials.
A machine that tells other machines the correct time.
A machine setting its clock by asking a time server every few minutes. It was paused on purpose during Kestrelmoor's March move.
A name given to one action before the first try, so a repeat with the same name is dropped. Here: the order number plus dispatch.
If the register asks you to charge a customer again, check the ticket number first. Name each action once, and let a repeat return the first result.
A switch that can cut a machine's power from outside it, so the machine can't stop it.

Checking a condition, then acting on it as a separate step. Anything that happens between the two can make the check out of date.

An international standard for running information security. Annex A 8.13 covers information backup and A.8.16 monitoring activities.

atWork: Look for the places where an old copy of a machine could wake up and act. A common pattern is a restored backup or a cloned machine, such as a virtual machine started from an old snapshot or a server image copied for a test, that comes up on the live network with its old work, its old clock and its old credentials. Read-only access is enough. First, list every place your services act on the world: the database, email and text senders, payment calls, outgoing webhooks, anything that moves a truck or money. For each, ask whether it checks a token or version and refuses older ones, or trusts whatever arrives. Second, find who grants ownership of work, and whether holders judge their lease on their own clock. Third, read your restore runbook: which network does a restored copy join, is that chosen by hand or copied from the snapshot, and is time sync on in the image? In AWS, check where test restores of EBS snapshots or AMIs are launched, and whether that VPC can reach production databases or message services. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A 8.13 (information backup) expects backups to be tested, which is the moment a restore can leak onto the live network, and A.8.16 (monitoring activities) covers spotting a machine nobody expected, like app-0 at 02:51. Flag for the design: a side effect with no token check, or restore tests that can reach production, would need rework before an audit, so build the check and the isolated restore network in from the first diagram.

recall.prompt: Your team restores last month's copy of a worker machine to check the backup works. Within a minute, customers get emails about jobs finished weeks ago, though the database rejected every one of the worker's writes. What happened, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The restored copy still believed it held its old lease, judged on its own stale clock: a zombie after a pause
The email sender checks no token; fencing only protects the places that check
Put a token check in front of the sender that refuses older tokens, and run restore tests on an isolated network

recall.model: The restored copy is a zombie after a pause. It woke mid-step from last month, still believed it held its old lease, and judged that lease on its own stale clock, so it carried on. The database refused its writes because it checks the fencing token, but the email sender checks no token, so every email went out. Fencing only protects the places that check. I'd put a gate in front of the email sender that keeps the newest token per job and refuses any older token, have the coordinator time leases on its own clock, give each email an idempotency key so a repeat is dropped, and run every restore test on an isolated test network with time sync on.

recall.prompt: In the sim, with everything else as built, which single change gets zero texts to drivers?
options: Power off before handover, app-0 unknown
Leases of 10 minutes instead of 60 seconds
A token gate in front of the texting service
recall.why: Only the gate checks the token where the texts leave: it holds 10 for batch #1102 and refuses app-0's 9 three times. Powering off needs someone to know app-0 is running; a longer lease just lets app-0 believe it owns the batch for 580 seconds; and the texting service had forgotten March's ticket numbers after 30 days.

recall.prompt: Why can't a machine stay safe by asking the coordinator whether its lease is valid right before it acts?
options: It can pause between the answer and the action, then act on a yes that's no longer true
The coordinator's clock is usually less accurate than the machine's
Asking takes longer than a lease lasts
The coordinator can't tell which machine holds each lease
recall.why: Check-then-act has a gap. A memory clean-up, a frozen host or a snapshot can stop the machine after the coordinator says yes and before the action, and by the time it acts the lease may belong to someone else. Only a check at the receiver, comparing tokens, closes the gap.

recall.model: A fencing token is a number the coordinator issues with every grant of a lease, and it always goes up, so the newest owner holds the highest. The holder sends it with every action. The receiver remembers the newest token it has seen for that piece of work and refuses any request with a token lower than that, whatever the sender believes. It must be checked at every place that acts on the world, not only the database: the texting or email service, payment calls, anything with a side effect. A place that doesn't check is a way out for a zombie, like a restored snapshot whose writes were refused but whose texts still reached drivers.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The gate has held: every restore test since November has run on the test network, and no stale text has reached a driver. In February we added delivery emails to customers, sent by app-1 to app-3 straight to an email company. On Tuesday 16 February 2027 app-2 froze for 75 seconds at 01:30. After 30 seconds of silence the Head of Shift declared it dead and gave its batch to app-3 with token 41, and when app-2 woke it finished two orders with token 40. The database refused both writes and the gate refused both texts. Two customers got two delivery emails each.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. The database and the gate both did their jobs, so why did two customers get two emails, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The emails are a new place that acts and they skip the gate; fencing only protects the places that check
Send emails through the gate too, refusing tokens older than the newest
Give each email a ticket number per order so a repeat is dropped

coldCase.model: app-2 became a zombie after a 75-second pause: it was declared dead after 30 seconds of silence, and acted with token 40 after app-3 got 41. The database and the gate refused it, but the emails go straight to the email company and skip the gate, and nothing there checks a token. Fencing only protects the places that check, and the emails were a new way out. Send every email through the gate too, so it refuses token 40 once it has seen 41, and give each email a ticket number made from the order, so a repeat from any machine is dropped as a repeat. Then add a rule for the future: any new way to act on the world goes behind the gate before it goes live.
